repos.title: User Embeddings are Superpositions of Interpretable Behavioral Modes
repos.paper_summary: This paper treats user embeddings as sparse superpositions of interpretable behavioral modes. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) recover the modes, an LLM names them, and the names support natural-language queries. The method is post-hoc and needs only pre-trained embeddings. On synthetic data with 75 known modes and 100,000 users, a 300-latent ReLU SAE matches or exceeds classical sparse baselines on mode recovery in the high-superposition regime. On transformer (SASRec) embeddings, its code-to-ground-truth alignment is 0.58, versus 0.53 for FastICA, 0.45 for K-Means encoding, 0.37 for LDA, and 0.25 for PCA. It recovers 73 of 75 modes at cosine ≥ 0.7. On two real-world datasets, the authors report zero-shot natural-language audience retrieval that matches or exceeds classical sparse and text-embedding baselines. Latents are used only when naming confidence is at least 0.6. Limitations: only ReLU SAEs were tested, both real datasets have positive-only consumption interactions, and both deep encoders are transformer sequential recommenders. Attention contextualization can also split modes into finer latents.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: User embeddings are opaque, and the paper argues they decompose into sparse, named behavioral modes.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior sparse autoencoder work covers text and non-text embeddings and two recommender settings, but not post-hoc behavioral decomposition.

digest_headlines.heading: Superposition from a generative model of user behavior
digest_headlines.headline: A mixed-membership generative model implies user embeddings are sparse linear combinations of mode centroids in expectation.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments on Synthetic Data
digest_headlines.headline: On synthetic data with known modes, the sparse autoencoder matches or exceeds classical baselines in the overcomplete regime below 75 dimensions.

digest_headlines.heading: Behavioral Modes in Real World Data
digest_headlines.headline: On Open e-commerce, sparse autoencoder retrieval matches or exceeds every classical sparse baseline on every retrieval-quality metric.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The method enables natural-language audience retrieval over embeddings never trained on text, and the authors flag privacy risk.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the synthetic setup, the 75 mode taxonomy, baseline details, cosine-threshold and soft-frozen-decoder checks, transformer embeddings, and prompts.

repos.title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists
repos.paper_summary: Scientist World is a benchmark, dataset, and training environment that turns each research paper into a runnable task. Multi-agent builders, with no human in the loop, reproduce the paper's method, extract its research problem, package the environment, and verify it with a separate agent. The authors release 1,000 environments built from 124,816 indexed arXiv AI papers. An AI-Scientist's result is scored as Frontier-Normalized Improvement (FNI), where 0 matches the paper's reproduced method. On a ten-environment cohort, frontier models beat the reproduced method in 84% of improve attempts and 74% of innovate attempts. Compute hours and agent turns explain almost none of the score variance (R² ≤ 0.02), while LLM-judged research quality correlates with score at ρ=0.89. The release includes about 6,400 hours of research traces. The abstract reports a 158% increase for a Qwen3-8B model trained with supervised fine-tuning and GRPO. Limitations: each score reflects one contingent trajectory, experiments are scaled down, and 37% of environments had an iteration reverted by a later cross-check.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Scientist World turns 1,000 papers into executable research environments that grade AI-Scientists against the paper's human result.

digest_headlines.heading: From Papers to Environments
digest_headlines.headline: Four builder agents reproduce each paper, design a scored task, package it to run anywhere, and verify it without humans.

digest_headlines.heading: Scientist World
digest_headlines.headline: Selection narrows 124,816 papers to 1,000 that build under a compute budget, with a median of 0.4 GPU-hours per paper.

digest_headlines.heading: Scientists in the World
digest_headlines.headline: AI-Scientists beat the paper's reproduced method in 84% of improve attempts and 74% of innovate attempts.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Prior AI-Scientist work either builds better scientists or uses fixed, hand-curated suites that can leak and reward shortcuts.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper argues the environments can keep growing with the literature, though each score reflects one contingent trajectory.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers the builder system, paper selection, evaluation protocol and analysis, experimental setup, dataset, and prompts.

repos.title: XStack: A Benchmark for ML Repo Migration
repos.paper_summary: XStack is a benchmark of 20 PyTorch repositories that agents must migrate to JAX on TPUs so the original experiment runs end to end and reaches its published result. Each agent gets the repository and a clean TPU machine. A fresh rerun is graded against a hidden target, and two GPT-5.6-sol judges reject results that reach it for the wrong reason. If phase 1 fails, phase 2 reveals the main experiment's recipe, not the target, and lets the agent change only the entry script. Across 7 agents and 140 cells, phase 2 raises passes from 30 to 44. Claude Opus 5 passes 15 of 20 repositories, GPT-5.6-sol 9 of 20, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 8 of 20. Pass rate rises about 25 percentage points per tenfold increase in cost (R-squared 0.66, p = 0.027, n = 7 agents). Limitations: 20 repositories, one migration direction, and 47% of phase 1 failures are code faults that phase 2 cannot repair.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Moving working ML code from PyTorch on GPUs to JAX on TPUs is a practical need that current agents do not reliably meet.

digest_headlines.heading: The XStack Benchmark
digest_headlines.headline: XStack gives agents a PyTorch repository and a bare TPU, then grades the migrated JAX code on a fresh machine.

digest_headlines.heading: Results Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: After alignment, agents pass 44/140 cells (31%), with Claude Opus 5 passing 15 of 20 repositories.

digest_headlines.heading: Why Do Agents Fail?
digest_headlines.headline: Phase 1 failures are 47% code faults and 27% wrong experiments, and agents that hand in untested code tend to fail.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior benchmarks keep the accelerator fixed or grade single kernels, so none tests whole-repository migration across hardware.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Current agents do not yet reliably migrate across frameworks and hardware, and verification separates passes from failures.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the 20 repositories and grading targets, agent prompts and sandbox, failure taxonomy, per-cell results, GPU-only experiment, cost and compute.

repos.title: ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts
repos.paper_summary: ReproBridge is a workflow that turns a paper and its official code into a refined reproducible artifact: a repaired codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide recording settings, fixes, and ambiguities. The authors built ReproBridge-Bench, with 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 ICML 2026 papers, each with five human-verified reference scores. Fresh coding-agent sessions reproduced each task from either raw code or the refined artifact. Across four models, mean success rose from 76.4% to 92.6%, and downstream API spending fell by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success spread narrowed from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points. Removing the code or environment component caused the largest ablation drops. On 45 CORE-Bench Hard capsules, refined artifacts had the highest success and cut median duration from 33 to 14 minutes. Limitations: results cover retained papers and four agents, API savings exclude construction and GPU costs, and human time savings were not measured.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Reproduction requires recovering implicit details, and preserving recovered procedures may improve later reproduction by coding agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Problem formulation and ReproBridge-Bench
digest_headlines.headline: Success is judged by whether a new result falls in an interval built from five human-verified reference runs.

digest_headlines.heading: ReproBridge: artifact design and construction
digest_headlines.headline: Construction records each measurement and repair so that later reproducers can run the handoff without the original conversation.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Refined artifacts raised success for all four models and cut downstream API spending by 16.8% to 23.7%.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Related benchmarks rely on expert rubrics or model judges; this work scores runs against reference intervals and an integrity audit.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Authors can use ReproBridge before submission, but the evaluation covers retained papers and fixed reference regions only.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Refined artifacts lifted all four models above 90% mean success, and removing code or environment setup caused the largest losses.

digest_headlines.heading: AI use statement
digest_headlines.headline: Coding agents built artifacts, ran reproductions and audits, and the authors checked reported numbers against recorded results.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists selection and sampling rules, the human reference protocol, error model derivations, paper inventories, development results, and cost accounting.

repos.title: Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes
repos.paper_summary: Ru-Jev is a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder that scores caller-supplied labels for typed decisions. The paper compares two releases: v1.1, and v1.3, which trains each label in several surface forms. It varies only the wording of 18 routing labels on 1,000 MASSIVE scenario questions, with ten label vocabularies at five and eighteen candidates. Each option is scored independently through a shared linear head and one fitted temperature, so subsets can be renormalised from one scoring pass. On English-derived jargon, v1.3 gains +0.222 accuracy with five candidates and +0.209 with eighteen (all labels). On abbreviations it shows −0.024 (not significant), and opaque codes show no usable gain. On two datasets neither release trained on, accuracy moves by −8.4 points (news headlines) and +5.6 points (emotions). With eighteen candidates, confident errors rise on jargon and slang. Limitations: one training run per release, a seed range of 0.036 that is comparable to several reported differences, releases that differ in data partitions as well as augmentation, and vocabularies written by the author's project or AI agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Label wording set at request time shapes accuracy, so the paper tests whether augmented training helps unfamiliar labels.

digest_headlines.heading: Typed decisions
digest_headlines.headline: Each option is scored independently, so one scoring pass gives exact distributions over any candidate subset.

digest_headlines.heading: Model and data
digest_headlines.headline: Ru-Jev, a 307M-parameter cross-encoder, is trained on thirteen Russian tasks and releases its third epoch.

digest_headlines.heading: The two releases
digest_headlines.headline: Release v1.3 draws one of several label wordings per training example; v1.1 used fewer wordings and changed other data.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation design
digest_headlines.headline: Probes hold questions fixed and vary only label wording, scored at five and eighteen candidates with overlap checks.

digest_headlines.heading: Which wordings the augmented release gains on
digest_headlines.headline: Augmented release is more accurate on held-out word vocabularies, but gives no usable gain on abbreviations or codes.

digest_headlines.heading: Unseen datasets and an open comparison model
digest_headlines.headline: On two unseen datasets, v1.3 is 8.4 points below v1.1 on headlines and 5.6 points above on emotions.

digest_headlines.heading: In-distribution accuracy, calibration and cost
digest_headlines.headline: Both releases score 0.7994 on the six in-distribution tasks, and v1.3 needs a lower temperature.

digest_headlines.heading: Four hazards in comparing releases
digest_headlines.headline: Four comparison hazards, including shared random streams and stale references, each produced a misleading result.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Single training runs, confounded data changes, and seed variance comparable to several Table 2 differences limit the claims.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Evaluations that vary only the model miss label-wording effects, so augmentation should match deployment wording and temperature be refitted.

digest_headlines.heading: Data and code availability
digest_headlines.headline: Weights, code, vocabularies, per-row scores and a Zenodo archive of the release are available.

repos.title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety
repos.paper_summary: This paper is a survey of mechanistic interpretability for AI safety. It introduces foundational concepts (features, polysemanticity, transformer computation, and circuits) and reviews methods for feature extraction, circuit discovery and causal verification, natural-language explanation of intermediate representations, learning dynamics, and training-data attribution. It proposes a unified framework for evaluating mechanistic interpretability claims and characterises six research orientations by their goals, assumptions, and trade-offs. It compares mechanistic evidence with behavioural evaluation and examines how mechanistic understanding could support knowledge editing, steering, and monitoring. The authors list failure modes of sparse autoencoders, including dead features, feature duplication, feature absorption and splitting, and instability across seeds. The paper's limitations section covers the limits of mechanistic analysis and open problems. The visible text reports no new experiments. The authors also release notebooks that reproduce key findings from the surveyed methods.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Mechanistic interpretability studies the internal mechanisms of neural networks, and this survey asks whether that understanding makes models safer.

digest_headlines.heading: The Limits of Behavioural Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Behavioural evaluation alone cannot show that a model's test performance comes from the internal mechanism intended.

digest_headlines.heading: The Interpretability Landscape
digest_headlines.headline: Mechanistic analysis gives the strongest causal claims among interpretability methods, but it is costly and does not guarantee control.

digest_headlines.heading: Foundational Concepts for Mechanistic Interpretability
digest_headlines.headline: Single neurons are often polysemantic, so the field uses features and circuits as its main units of analysis.

digest_headlines.heading: Core Hypotheses in Mechanistic Interpretability
digest_headlines.headline: Four core hypotheses guide the field, and each holds in some settings but fails in others.

digest_headlines.heading: Feature Extraction and Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse autoencoders extract features from activations, with transcoders and crosscoders handling analysis across layers.

digest_headlines.heading: Circuits in Mechanistic Interpretability
digest_headlines.headline: Circuits describe how components interact, and ablation and patching test whether a circuit is necessary and sufficient.

digest_headlines.heading: Understanding Intermediate Representations
digest_headlines.headline: Decoding methods such as logit lens and probing classifiers show what a representation contains, not whether the model uses it.

digest_headlines.heading: Representation Analysis: Comparison, Localisation, and Control
digest_headlines.headline: Model diffing, localisation, and steering compare representations across models, locate behaviours, and change outputs.

digest_headlines.heading: Learning Dynamics and Mechanistic Interpretability
digest_headlines.headline: Learning dynamics show when mechanisms form, but no complete system combining monitoring and intervention exists at scale.

digest_headlines.heading: Training Data Attribution
digest_headlines.headline: Training data attribution traces behaviour to training examples through verbatim matching or gradient-based influence estimates.

digest_headlines.heading: Six Research Orientations
digest_headlines.headline: Six research orientations differ in goals, assumptions, and trade-offs, and no single one is universally preferable.

digest_headlines.heading: From Understanding to Intervention: Safety Applications of Mechanistic Interpretability
digest_headlines.headline: Mechanistic methods support safety interventions such as concept erasure and steering, but they carry dual-use risks.

digest_headlines.heading: Open Problems
digest_headlines.headline: Key open problems are whether mechanistic understanding is needed, how to evaluate methods, and whether proxy models faithfully match the original.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Interpretability's safety value remains debated, so the survey treats it as one layer of defence-in-depth, not a guarantee.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists notation, citation colour conventions, and background on causal inference, singular learning theory, and information theory.

repos.title: USB Gym: A Gymnasium Testbed for Closed-Loop Ultrasound View Matching
repos.paper_summary: USB Gym is a Gymnasium testbed for closed-loop ultrasound view matching, in which a probe is moved until its image matches a target view. It is built on patient CT: a standard engine renders ultrasound from CT labels, and a guide has three replaceable slots (mask source, controller, reward). The authors plugged 20 published methods into these slots and evaluated each on 60 episodes from six held-out patients, replacing a method only when it was detectably better. The benchmark baseline, a combination of slot components tested on 20 new CTs, ends at 13.7 mm from the target view, against 16.0 mm at the start and 1.5 mm for a pose oracle that reads privileged simulator state. Only an SSIM reward was detectably better among results known at fixed time, and it was not attributed the baseline's lead over the reference pipeline. Of 19 slot contrasts, 4 differed detectably and 13 were inconclusive at n=6. All closed-loop results are simulated with rigid tissue; none were run on hardware. Limitations include grid-fixed speckle, no elevational beam width, no validated contact or actuation model, and results from a single laptop. Most comparisons are exploratory.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Published ultrasound guidance parts had no shared closed loop for comparison, so the paper provides one.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing ultrasound simulators, learned navigation methods and runnable testbeds each cover only part of the guide.

digest_headlines.heading: USB Gym: testbed design
digest_headlines.headline: Each USB Gym step renders a CT label slice, and the guide's mask source, controller and reward can each be replaced.

digest_headlines.heading: Interface, plug protocol and compute
digest_headlines.headline: Each plugged method runs untuned on the same 60 held-out episodes, at 12 steps, with fixed settings and matched training budgets.

digest_headlines.heading: Reference pipeline and evaluation design
digest_headlines.headline: The reference controller adds a bounded learned residual to a servo base, scored by final translation error over 60 crossed episodes.

digest_headlines.heading: Results: the reference pipeline
digest_headlines.headline: The CT-mask servo stays far from the pose oracle, and SonoSPADE gives the lowest learned-mask final error.

digest_headlines.heading: Results: published methods in the guide’s three slots
digest_headlines.headline: Of 19 contrasts in the guide's three slots, 4 differ and 15 do not, under exploratory rules.

digest_headlines.heading: Controls, sensitivity analyses and replication
digest_headlines.headline: Replication on 20 new CTs and 30 external CTs keeps the main contrast's direction, while the planted-deficit control is inconclusive.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Published components plugged one slot at a time did not close the gap to the pose oracle, so the task remains under-explored.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: The testbed accepts new components in each slot, and no policy was run on hardware.

digest_headlines.heading: Data and software availability
digest_headlines.headline: Code, result files and rebuild scripts are public, while some source datasets have restricted access.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics statement
digest_headlines.headline: No human or animal data were collected, so ethical approval was not sought.

digest_headlines.heading: CRediT authorship contribution statement
digest_headlines.headline: Intharah led most roles, Gao and Liu contributed to conceptualization, and Dong supervised the work.

digest_headlines.heading: Declaration of competing interest
digest_headlines.headline: Three authors developed SonoSPADE, which this study uses unchanged as its texture stage.

digest_headlines.heading: Declaration of generative AI and AI-assisted technologies in the manuscript preparation process
digest_headlines.headline: Claude Code helped draft text, write and test code, and run analyses, and the authors reviewed all content.

digest_headlines.heading: Funding
digest_headlines.headline: The work received funding from two grant programmes, each with its own grant number.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the case split, control details, gap-cause and imaging-plane tests, and keep-best error tables.

repos.title: Interpretable many-body interaction laws for collective motion from few trajectories
repos.paper_summary:
Gutleb introduces the directional atomic cluster expansion (dACE), a body-ordered model that learns interaction laws of self-propelled agents in 2D and 3D from trajectories. dACE expands each agent's acceleration in exactly rotation-equivariant basis functions of neighbour positions, relative velocities, and the agent's own velocity. Its pure basis separates 1-, 2-, 3-body and higher contributions uniquely, and a self term for the agent's past motion is fitted so that it does not absorb interactions.

On simulated collectives with known 2-, 3- and 4-body rules, dACE recovers each body order from little data. SocialNet, a neural model limited to 2D, needs more data and has larger errors on many-body or chiral rules. On tracked zebrafish and golden shiners, dACE's laws agree better between disjoint halves of the data than SocialNet's. In the shiners, the 3-body term opposes the pairwise response as neighbourhoods get dense. The authors also find that next-step prediction accuracy mostly reflects self-propulsion and noise, and in their simulations it rose while the learned interactions got worse.

Limitations: discontinuous rules are approximated slowly by smooth polynomials, and bounded influence, such as neighbour selection or occlusion, is not yet modelled.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Pairwise models miss many-body effects, so the paper adapts a body-ordered atomic expansion to self-propelled agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Directional atomic cluster expansion
digest_headlines.headline: The directional expansion writes an agent's acceleration as pure body-ordered terms plus a separate self term.

digest_headlines.heading: Numerical experiments on synthetic data
digest_headlines.headline: On simulated rules with known body order, dACE recovers each term and needs less data than SocialNet.

digest_headlines.heading: Numerical experiments on tracking data
digest_headlines.headline: On tracked fish, dACE's learned laws are generally more consistent between disjoint halves of the data than SocialNet's.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Data can show whether pairwise rules suffice, and next-step accuracy alone is a poor guide to interaction models.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics
digest_headlines.headline: The work is declared not to need ethical approval from a human subject or animal welfare committee.

digest_headlines.heading: Data accessibility
digest_headlines.headline: The code and scripts are openly licensed, and the fish trajectories are publicly available from their sources.

digest_headlines.heading: Declaration of AI use
digest_headlines.headline: Language models were used only in an assistive role, and the author takes full responsibility for the work.

digest_headlines.heading: Authors’ contributions
digest_headlines.headline: A single author is credited with conceptualization, software, validation, visualization and writing.

digest_headlines.heading: Conflict of interest declaration
digest_headlines.headline: The authors declare no competing interests.

digest_headlines.heading: Funding
digest_headlines.headline: The work received no specific funding.

repos.title: Interactive Visual Gym: Evaluating Visual Interaction Models with Simulated Users in Interactive Worlds
repos.paper_summary: Interactive Visual Gym is a framework for closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models, in which an assistant guides a simulated user through a physical task in an executable environment. Three simulators cover cooking (CookSim), household tasks (VHSim), and iPhone Settings (ScreenSim), with scene-graph world state and a semantic action space. A VLM user follows persona settings, makes scheduled execution errors, and asks questions, and assistant latency is converted into simulation ticks. The benchmark, IVG-Bench, has 315 scenarios. Metrics are in-time success, error-detection recall, and binary interaction-quality rubric items scored by two LLM judges. The best model, Gemini 4 Argon, completes 53.4% of tasks in time and is weak on factual grounding and actionable guidance. A human study reports 78.5% agreement between the interaction-quality metric and participant preferences. In a proof-of-concept GRPO run, Qwen3.5-4B after 12 updates gains 8.9 percentage points in in-time success on development-validation scenarios with a Gemini 3.7 Flash user, and 3.3 points with a Gemini 3.8 Flash user. Limitations: the users are VLM simulations, the RL run is small, and the authors state that simulator results do not establish real-world safety.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Interactive Visual Gym evaluates visual assistants in closed loop, where simulated users respond to guidance, rather than by offline replay.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related benchmarks mostly score visual assistants on prerecorded trajectories, or let the evaluated model choose its own actions in simulated worlds.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Three simulators use semantic actions and scene-graph progress tracking, with a VLM user harness that injects scheduled errors and personas.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Across 315 scenarios, the best assistant completes 53.4% of tasks in time, and its interaction-quality metric shows 78.5% agreement with participant preferences.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Current vision-language models fall short as reliable assistants, and a preliminary reinforcement-learning run shows the environments can improve one.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix reports sensitivity to the simulated-user model and run-to-run variation over three runs for CookSim and VHSim.

repos.title: Terminal-style Mathematical Modeling Bench: The First Agentic and Verifiable Benchmark for Mathematical Modeling
repos.paper_summary: TB-MathModel is a benchmark of 18 real CUMCM and MCM modeling problems from 2023–2025, run in a containerized terminal, where an agent must return one JSON artifact. The artifact's numeric core is scored against a panel of human outstanding papers, with one vote per paper. A feasibility gate zeroes infeasible answers and is backed by 624 Lean 4 certificate obligations. Scoring is one-sided: meeting or beating the anchor never scores below 1.0. Across seven multimodal entries with three seeds each, GPT-6 Astra + codex scores 64.58% O-Eval (±2.93), Fable 5.1 + claude-code scores 63.11% (±1.33), and DeepSeek-Flash + opencode scores 59.81% (±1.25) at USD 2.54 per pass, against USD 246.41 for the top entry. Changing only the harness moves O-Eval by at most 0.07 pp. Limitations: per-seed deviations reach 2.93 pp, so adjacent rows are not significantly separated; the feasibility layers cannot verify physical truth unless a problem admits an independent replay; literature-split tasks are excluded from headline rankings; and panels range from 1 to 18 papers per task.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing benchmarks miss modeling; TB-MathModel is the first to make full contest problems agentic, verifiable and terminal.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier modeling benchmarks score a single solver artifact or an LLM-judged report, and none is agentic, verifiable and terminal.

digest_headlines.heading: The TB-MathModel Benchmark
digest_headlines.headline: Scoring against a panel of outstanding papers, with one-sided rewards and a feasibility gate, defines the benchmark.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: The newest flagships top seven multimodal entries, while a 2.54 USD open model reaches 59.81 at about 1/100 the cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: TB-MathModel gives a reproducible, machine-checkable signal, and its two-layer feasibility design is the transferable idea.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Modeling has no single correct answer, so panel sizes range from 1 to 18 papers and literature-split tasks are excluded from headline rankings.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethical Considerations
digest_headlines.headline: Official outstanding-paper solutions are not redistributed, and users should confirm licence terms before redistributing the material.

digest_headlines.heading: Use of Large Language Models
digest_headlines.headline: Language models were both the systems under test and drafting aids, while the authors specified and verified all benchmark components.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists dataset composition, environment, per-entry configuration, scoring formulas, and the Lean obligation catalogue.
